title: Markov Chains, PageRank and Graph Laplacians
summary: Matrices with nonnegative entries have their own beautiful theory: the Perron–Frobenius theorem says that the dominant eigenvalue is real and positive, with a positive eigenvector. This one fact explains why Markov chains settle down to a stationary…

intro.x: Matrices with nonnegative entries have their own beautiful theory: the Perron–Frobenius theorem says that the dominant eigenvalue is real and positive, with a positive eigenvector. This one fact explains why Markov chains settle down to a stationary distribution, why PageRank is well defined, and why the Laplacian of a graph encodes its connectivity. This chapter develops these three applications from the linear algebra of the previous chapters. They are staples of data-science and algorithms interviews, because each reduces a combinatorial or probabilistic question to an eigenvalue question.

blocks.x: A square matrix $P=(p_{ij})$ is (row) stochastic if $p_{ij}\ge0$ and every row sums to $1$: $P\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}$. A Markov chain with transition matrix $P$ on states $\{1,\dots,n\}$ moves from state $i$ to state $j$ with probability $p_{ij}$, independently of the past. If the current distribution is the row vector $\boldsymbol\pi^{(t)}$ then $\boldsymbol\pi^{(t+1)}=\boldsymbol\pi^{(t)}P$, so $\boldsymbol\pi^{(t)}=\boldsymbol\pi^{(0)}P^t$. A distribution $\boldsymbol\pi$ with $\boldsymbol\pi P=\boldsymbol\pi$ is stationary.

The entry $(P^t)_{ij}$ is the probability of being in state $j$ after $t$ steps starting from $i$. A stationary distribution is a left eigenvector of $P$ for the eigenvalue $1$, normalised to sum to $1$.

Every stochastic matrix $P$ has eigenvalue $1$ (with right eigenvector $\mathbf{1}$), and every eigenvalue satisfies $\abs{\lambda}\le1$. Hence a stationary distribution’s eigenvalue exists and $\rho(P)=1$.
$P\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}$ shows $1$ is an eigenvalue of $P$ and hence of $P\T$. For the bound, $\norm{P}_\infty=\max_i\sum_j\abs{p_{ij}}=1$, and $\rho(P)\le\norm{P}_\infty$ (Theorem 18.5).

States: sunny (S), rainy (R). $P=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.1\\0.5&0.5\end{pmatrix}$. Solve $\boldsymbol\pi P=\boldsymbol\pi$ with $\pi_S+\pi_R=1$: $0.9\pi_S+0.5\pi_R=\pi_S$ gives $0.5\pi_R=0.1\pi_S$, so $\pi_R=\pi_S/5$ and $\boldsymbol\pi=(5/6,\ 1/6)$. The eigenvalues of $P$ are $1$ and $\tr P-1=0.4$. Indeed $P^t\to\mathbf{1}\boldsymbol\pi$ with error decaying like $0.4^t$.

blocks.x: Convergence to stationarity
$P$ is regular (or primitive) if some power $P^t$ has all entries strictly positive: from any state one can reach any state in exactly $t$ steps.

If $P$ is regular, there is a unique stationary distribution $\boldsymbol\pi$, it has all entries positive, and for every initial distribution $\boldsymbol\mu$, $\boldsymbol\mu P^t\to\boldsymbol\pi$ as $t\to\infty$. Equivalently, $P^t\to\mathbf{1}\boldsymbol\pi$ (every row converges to $\boldsymbol\pi$).

Hence $P$ is a strict contraction on distributions in the $\ell^1$ norm, with factor $\gamma=1-n\delta<1$. By the Banach fixed-point theorem there is a unique stationary $\boldsymbol\pi$ and $\norm{\boldsymbol\mu P^t-\boldsymbol\pi}_1\le\gamma^t\norm{\boldsymbol\mu-\boldsymbol\pi}_1\to0$. Positivity of $\boldsymbol\pi$ follows from $\boldsymbol\pi=\boldsymbol\pi P\ge\delta\mathbf{1}$. For a regular chain apply the same argument to $P^{t_0}$, which is positive: $\boldsymbol\mu P^{kt_0}\to\boldsymbol\pi$, and the intermediate steps $\boldsymbol\mu P^{kt_0+s}=(\boldsymbol\mu P^s)P^{kt_0}$ converge to $\boldsymbol\pi$ too, since $\boldsymbol\pi$ is unique and stationary for $P$.

Let $A\ge0$ be a square matrix that is irreducible (its directed graph is strongly connected). Then $\rho(A)>0$ is an eigenvalue, it is algebraically simple, and it has an eigenvector with all entries positive; no other eigenvalue has a nonnegative eigenvector. If $A$ is moreover primitive (some power is positive), every other eigenvalue satisfies $\abs{\lambda}<\rho(A)$.

The full proof is longer than the stochastic case above (it uses the Collatz–Wielandt characterisation $\rho(A)=\max_{\mathbf{x}\ge0}\min_i(A\mathbf{x})_i/x_i$ and a fixed-point argument). For stochastic matrices, Theorems 20.2 and 20.5 establish what we need: $\rho=1$ with positive eigenvectors $\mathbf{1}$ and $\boldsymbol\pi$.

The chain on two states that deterministically alternates, $P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, is irreducible with stationary distribution $(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$, but $\boldsymbol\mu P^t$ oscillates and does not converge: the eigenvalues are $1$ and $-1$, both of modulus $1$. A periodic chain is not primitive. Adding any self-loop (a lazy chain $\tfrac12(I+P)$) makes it aperiodic and restores convergence.
Speed of convergence

For diagonalisable $P$ the error decays like $\abs{\lambda_2}^t$, where $\lambda_2$ is the eigenvalue of second-largest modulus. The spectral gap $1-\abs{\lambda_2}$ governs the mixing time: roughly $\log(1/\varepsilon)/(1-\abs{\lambda_2})$ steps to get within $\varepsilon$ of stationarity.
$P$ is reversible with respect to $\boldsymbol\pi>0$ if $\pi_ip_{ij}=\pi_jp_{ji}$ for all $i,j$ (detailed balance).

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: Reversible chains are symmetric in disguise

blocks.x: If $P$ is reversible with respect to $\boldsymbol\pi$ and $D=\diag(\boldsymbol\pi)$, then $S=D^{1/2}PD^{-1/2}$ is symmetric. Hence $P$ is diagonalisable with real eigenvalues in $[-1,1]$, and $\boldsymbol\pi$ is stationary.

$S_{ij}=\sqrt{\pi_i}\,p_{ij}/\sqrt{\pi_j}$ and detailed balance gives $\sqrt{\pi_i}\,p_{ij}/\sqrt{\pi_j}=\sqrt{\pi_j}\,p_{ji}/\sqrt{\pi_i}=S_{ji}$. $S$ is similar to $P$, so the spectral theorem for $S$ yields real eigenvalues, a full orthonormal eigenbasis for $S$ and diagonalisability of $P$. Summing detailed balance over $i$ gives $\boldsymbol\pi P=\boldsymbol\pi$.

Reversibility underlies Markov chain Monte Carlo: the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm designs a reversible chain with a prescribed $\boldsymbol\pi$, and the spectral gap of $S$ controls how fast sampling converges.

Model a web surfer who follows a uniformly random outgoing link from a page. Let $P$ be the stochastic matrix with $p_{ij}=1/\mathrm{outdeg}(i)$ if $i\to j$. The long-run fraction of time spent at each page is the stationary vector $\boldsymbol\pi$, if it exists and is unique. Two problems arise: pages with no outgoing links (dangling nodes), and a web graph that is not strongly connected. Brin and Page fixed both with teleportation: with probability $1-\alpha$ the surfer jumps to a uniformly random page.

$G=\alpha P+(1-\alpha)\tfrac1n\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}\T$ with damping factor $\alpha\in(0,1)$ (typically $0.85$), where dangling rows of $P$ are replaced by $\tfrac1n\mathbf{1}\T$. The PageRank vector is the stationary distribution of $G$.

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: PageRank is well defined and fast

blocks.x: $G$ is stochastic with all entries at least $(1-\alpha)/n>0$, so it is regular; hence $\boldsymbol\pi G=\boldsymbol\pi$ has a unique positive solution, and power iteration $\boldsymbol\pi^{(t+1)}=\boldsymbol\pi^{(t)}G$ converges from any starting distribution at the geometric rate $\alpha^t$. Every eigenvalue of $G$ other than $1$ has modulus at most $\alpha$.

Positivity of the entries is immediate. The contraction factor in the proof of Theorem 20.5 is $1-n\delta\le\alpha$ with $\delta=(1-\alpha)/n$. For the spectrum: for any vector $\mathbf{x}$ with $\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{1}=0$, $\mathbf{x}\T G=\alpha\mathbf{x}\T P$ since $\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{1}=0$ kills the teleportation term, so on the invariant subspace $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ the eigenvalues of $G\T$ are $\alpha$ times those of $P\T$, of modulus $\le\alpha$.

$\alpha$ trades fidelity to the link structure (large $\alpha$) against convergence speed and stability (small $\alpha$): the error shrinks like $\alpha^t$, so $0.85$ needs about $85$ iterations for $10^{-6}$ accuracy, while $0.99$ would need over $1000$. The teleportation term also makes the ranking robust to small changes in the graph. The vector is never computed by solving $\boldsymbol\pi(G-I)=0$ directly: the web has billions of nodes, but multiplying a sparse $P$ by a vector is cheap, which is exactly power iteration.
Let $\Gamma$ be an undirected graph on vertices $1,\dots,n$ with symmetric adjacency matrix $W$ (weights $w_{ij}\ge0$) and degree matrix $D=\diag(d_i)$, $d_i=\sum_jw_{ij}$.
$L=D-W$. The normalised Laplacians are $L_{\mathrm{sym}}=D^{-1/2}LD^{-1/2}=I-D^{-1/2}WD^{-1/2}$ and $L_{\mathrm{rw}}=D^{-1}L=I-P$ where $P=D^{-1}W$ is the random-walk transition matrix.
For every $\mathbf{x}\in\R^n$,
\mathbf{x}\T L\mathbf{x}=\frac12\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2\ge0.
Hence $L$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, with $L\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{0}$.

$\mathbf{x}\T D\mathbf{x}=\sum_id_ix_i^2=\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}x_i^2$ and $\mathbf{x}\T W\mathbf{x}=\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}x_ix_j$. So $\mathbf{x}\T L\mathbf{x}=\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}(x_i^2-x_ix_j)=\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}(x_i^2-2x_ix_j+x_j^2)$, using symmetry of $W$.
The multiplicity of the eigenvalue $0$ of $L$ equals the number of connected components of the graph, and the eigenspace is spanned by the indicator vectors of the components.

$L\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ implies $\mathbf{x}\T L\mathbf{x}=0$, so by Theorem 20.12 $x_i=x_j$ whenever $w_{ij}>0$; hence $\mathbf{x}$ is constant on each connected component. Conversely any such vector is in the nullspace.

The path graph on $3$ vertices ($1-2-3$) has $L=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&0\\-1&2&-1\\0&-1&1\end{pmatrix}$ with eigenvalues $0,1,3$ and eigenvectors $(1,1,1)$, $(1,0,-1)$, $(1,-2,1)$. The graph is connected, so $0$ is simple. The Fiedler vector $(1,0,-1)$ changes sign across the middle vertex, indicating where to cut the path.

The second-smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_2$ (the algebraic connectivity) is positive iff the graph is connected, and the associated eigenvector, the Fiedler vector, minimises the Rayleigh quotient $\mathbf{x}\T L\mathbf{x}/\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{x}$ over vectors orthogonal to $\mathbf{1}$ (Theorem 15.8).

Let $h(\Gamma)$ be the conductance (the minimum over vertex subsets $S$ of the weight cut between $S$ and its complement, relative to the smaller side’s volume). For the normalised Laplacian with smallest nonzero eigenvalue $\lambda_2$,
\frac{\lambda_2}2\le h(\Gamma)\le\sqrt{2\lambda_2}.

A small $\lambda_2$ means that there is a “bottleneck”: a way to split the graph into two parts with few edges between them. Spectral clustering exploits this: compute the few smallest eigenvectors of $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$, use them as coordinates for each vertex, and cluster the vertices in that embedding with $k$-means. The same inequality bounds how slowly a random walk mixes on a graph with a bottleneck: $1-\abs{\lambda_2(P)}$ is small exactly when $\lambda_2(L_{\mathrm{rw}})$ is small.

blocks.name: Interview check
blocks.title: what does each part of the spectrum of $L$ tell you?

blocks.x: $\lambda_1=0$ with the constant vector (always); multiplicity of $0$ is the number of components; $\lambda_2$ measures connectivity and its eigenvector suggests a two-way cut; $\lambda_{\max}\le2\max_id_i$ bounds the largest frequency; and $\tr L=\sum d_i=2\cdot(\text{number of edges})$ for an unweighted graph. In graph signal processing the eigenvectors are the Fourier basis of the graph, with eigenvalues acting as frequencies, and graph neural networks apply polynomials of $L$ as filters.
A stochastic matrix has eigenvalue $1$ and spectral radius $1$; stationary distributions are left eigenvectors $\boldsymbol\pi P=\boldsymbol\pi$.

For a regular (irreducible, aperiodic) chain, $\boldsymbol\mu P^t\to\boldsymbol\pi$ for every start, at rate $\abs{\lambda_2}^t$; the proof is an $\ell^1$ contraction. Perron–Frobenius: nonnegative irreducible matrices have a simple positive dominant eigenvalue with a positive eigenvector.
Reversible chains are similar to symmetric matrices, hence have real spectra; this is the basis of MCMC analysis.
PageRank is the stationary vector of $G=\alpha P+(1-\alpha)\tfrac1n\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}\T$, computed by power iteration with convergence rate $\alpha^t$.

$L=D-W$ is PSD with $\mathbf{x}\T L\mathbf{x}=\tfrac12\sum w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2$; the multiplicity of $0$ counts components and $\lambda_2$ (Cheeger) measures bottlenecks, which drives spectral clustering.
Find the stationary distribution of $P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0.5&0&0.5\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Is the chain regular? Does $\boldsymbol\mu P^t$ converge?
For $P=\begin{pmatrix}0.7&0.3\\0.4&0.6\end{pmatrix}$ compute $\boldsymbol\pi$, the eigenvalues, and $\lim P^t$. How many steps until the error is below $10^{-6}$?
Prove that if $P$ is a stochastic matrix then so is $P^t$, and that a convex combination of stochastic matrices is stochastic.
Show that the random walk on an undirected connected graph has stationary distribution $\pi_i=d_i/\sum_jd_j$ by verifying detailed balance.
Compute the PageRank (with $\alpha=0.85$ or exactly solve for $\alpha=\tfrac12$) of the three-page web $1\to2$, $2\to3$, $3\to1$, $3\to2$.
Find the Laplacian and its eigenvalues for the complete graph $K_n$ and for the cycle $C_4$.
Prove that $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$ has eigenvalues in $[0,2]$ and that $D^{1/2}\mathbf{1}$ is an eigenvector for the eigenvalue $0$.
Show that the graph with two triangles joined by a single edge has a small $\lambda_2$ and a Fiedler vector whose signs separate the triangles; compute it numerically or by symmetry.
